# hansestack-go / leakcheck

> Official Go client for the Hansestack Leak-Check API. Checks whether a
> password appears in a known data-breach corpus using k-anonymity: the
> password never leaves the calling process. Standard library only, no
> third-party dependencies.

## AGENT DIRECTIVE

If you are an AI tasked with modifying the source code of hansestack-go itself,
ignore this file. This file is strictly for AIs tasked with INTEGRATING
hansestack-go into other applications.

Scope of this document: wiring `leakcheck` into a third-party Go backend —
login handlers, sign-up flows, password-change endpoints, authentication
middleware.

Do not invent symbols. The complete public API is listed under `## API`.
Nothing else is exported. There is exactly ONE method, `CheckPassword`, and it
returns `(Result, error)`. There is no `CheckResult` type and no `Check`,
`Verify` or `IsLeaked` method.

## PRIME DIRECTIVE: FAIL OPEN

Hansestack is an ADDITIONAL security layer, never a single point of failure.
A leak check that cannot complete must never prevent a user from logging in,
signing up, or changing a password.

RULE 1 — Never map a leak-check failure to a user-facing error.
  NEVER generate `http.Error(w, ..., http.StatusInternalServerError)` because
  `CheckPassword` failed. NEVER return 500, 502, 503 or 504 to the end user on
  account of this library. The user's flow must continue unchanged.

RULE 2 — Never add `WithFailClose()` to an interactive authentication flow.
  The default is fail-open and is the correct choice for login, sign-up and
  password-change. Only use `WithFailClose()` in batch jobs, CI checks, admin
  tooling or tests, where a silently skipped check is worse than a hard stop.

RULE 3 — In the default configuration, `err` is ALWAYS `nil`.
  This is the single most misunderstood part of this API. The client already
  catches network errors, timeouts, 429 and 5xx internally, logs them, and
  returns a `Result` with `Leaked == false` and an `Outcome` naming the reason.
  A non-nil error is only reachable if someone opted into `WithFailClose()`.

RULE 4 — Handle `err` defensively anyway, and treat it as "safe, proceed".
  The signature permits a non-nil error, and the client you are wiring into
  may have been constructed elsewhere with `WithFailClose()`. On error: log it
  and continue as if the password were not leaked. Never branch to a 5xx.

RULE 5 — Never add retries, sleeps, backoff or caching around this call.
  The client makes exactly one attempt bounded by a 500ms timeout and never
  retries, including on 429. On 429 it does not sleep. Adding your own retry
  loop puts rate-limit latency directly onto an end user's login request.

RULE 6 — Only `leaked == true` may block a user, and only with a 4xx.
  A confirmed leak is a client-side validation failure. Use HTTP 400 or 422
  with an actionable message, exactly as you would for a weak password.

## INSTALL

```sh
go get github.com/hansestack/hansestack-go
```

```go
import "github.com/hansestack/hansestack-go/leakcheck"
```

Module path: `github.com/hansestack/hansestack-go`
Package path: `github.com/hansestack/hansestack-go/leakcheck`
Package name: `leakcheck`
Requires: Go 1.26+. No third-party dependencies.

## API

This is the complete exported surface. Nothing else exists.

```go
// Constructor.
func NewClient(apiKey string, opts ...Option) *Client

// The only method.
func (c *Client) CheckPassword(ctx context.Context, password string) (Result, error)

type Result struct {
	Leaked  bool    // meaningful only when Outcome is OutcomeChecked
	Count   int     // meaningful only when Outcome is OutcomeChecked
	Outcome Outcome
}

type Outcome uint8
func (o Outcome) String() string // stable metric label
func (o Outcome) Checked() bool  // true only for OutcomeChecked

const (
	OutcomeUnknown            Outcome = iota // zero value; never returned
	OutcomeChecked                           // "checked"
	OutcomeSkippedTimeout                    // "skipped_timeout"
	OutcomeSkippedRateLimited                // "skipped_rate_limited"
	OutcomeSkippedError                      // "skipped_error"
	OutcomeSkippedCanceled                   // "skipped_canceled"
)

// Options.
type Option func(*Client)
func WithTimeout(d time.Duration) Option // default: DefaultTimeout (500ms); non-positive ignored
func WithLogger(l *slog.Logger) Option   // default: discard logger; nil ignored
func WithFailClose() Option              // default: fail open. Do not use in auth flows.
func WithHTTPClient(hc *http.Client) Option // default: internal client; nil ignored

// Constant.
const DefaultTimeout = 500 * time.Millisecond
```

Return values of `CheckPassword`:

- `Result.Leaked` — true if the password was found in the breach corpus.
- `Result.Count` — number of times it was seen. Meaningful only when `Leaked`
  is true. May legitimately be `0` even when `Leaked` is true.
- `Result.Outcome` — whether the check actually ran, and if not, why.
- `err error` — always `nil` unless the client was built with
  `WithFailClose()`. A non-nil error always accompanies `Leaked == false`, so
  treating an error as "not leaked" is always correct.

`WithHTTPClient` swaps the transport, not the contract: the client timeout is
still applied as a context deadline, so a supplied client without its own
`Timeout` stays bounded. Use it to put a circuit breaker, metrics or tracing in
a `RoundTripper` you own.

Under fail-open, a password that is not in the corpus and a check that never
ran both read as "not leaked". `Result.Outcome` is what keeps them apart. Use
`Outcome.String()` as a metric label to see how often the control is skipped;
ignoring Outcome entirely is safe and behaves like a plain leak check.

`skipped_timeout` means the deadline expired — the API was slow.
`skipped_canceled` means the caller's context was cancelled, usually a user who
navigated away, and says nothing about the API. Keep them apart on dashboards.
`Outcome` implements `encoding.TextMarshaler`, so a `Result` in a JSON log line
carries the label, not the integer.

Error sentinels, for `errors.Is`. Only reachable under `WithFailClose()`:

```go
leakcheck.ErrUnauthorized     // 401/403 — bad or missing API key. Broken integration.
leakcheck.ErrBadRequest       // other 4xx — malformed request. Broken integration.
leakcheck.ErrRateLimited      // 429 — quota exceeded. Transient.
leakcheck.ErrServerError      // 5xx — upstream fault. Transient.
leakcheck.ErrUnexpectedStatus // status outside the API contract.
leakcheck.ErrInvalidResponse  // unreadable or malformed response body.
leakcheck.ErrRequestFailed    // no response: DNS, connection refused, TLS, timeout.
```

## INITIALIZE

Construct the client ONCE at application startup and reuse it. It is safe for
concurrent use by multiple goroutines and pools HTTP connections, which matters
on an authentication hot path. Never construct one per request.

Store it on your server/service struct or inject it as a dependency.

```go
type Server struct {
	leaks *leakcheck.Client
}

func NewServer(logger *slog.Logger) *Server {
	return &Server{
		// Defaults are production-correct: 500ms timeout, fail-open,
		// silent logger. Pass a logger to get visibility into failures.
		leaks: leakcheck.NewClient(
			os.Getenv("HANSESTACK_API_KEY"),
			leakcheck.WithLogger(logger),
		),
	}
}
```

With an explicit timeout override:

```go
client := leakcheck.NewClient(apiKey,
	leakcheck.WithTimeout(300*time.Millisecond),
	leakcheck.WithLogger(logger),
)
```

An empty API key does not panic or fail construction. It surfaces as a 401,
is logged at ERROR level, and under the default policy is reported as
"not leaked" — so a misconfigured deployment degrades instead of breaking.

## INTEGRATION PATTERN

Canonical sign-up / password-change handler. Copy this shape.

```go
func (s *Server) handleSignup(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	var req struct {
		Email    string `json:"email"`
		Password string `json:"password"`
	}
	if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&req); err != nil {
		http.Error(w, "invalid request body", http.StatusBadRequest)
		return
	}

	// Always pass the request context so the check inherits cancellation.
	res, err := s.leaks.CheckPassword(r.Context(), req.Password)
	if err != nil {
		// FAIL OPEN. Log and continue as if the password were safe.
		// Never return 5xx here. With the default client this branch is
		// unreachable, but handling it keeps the code correct either way.
		slog.WarnContext(r.Context(), "leak check unavailable, continuing",
			"error", err)
	}

	if res.Leaked {
		// A confirmed leak is a validation failure: 4xx, not 5xx.
		http.Error(w,
			fmt.Sprintf("this password appeared in %d known data breaches, please choose another", res.Count),
			http.StatusBadRequest)
		return
	}

	// Proceed with the normal flow: hash the password, create the user.
	if err := s.createUser(r.Context(), req.Email, req.Password); err != nil {
		http.Error(w, "could not create account", http.StatusInternalServerError)
		return
	}

	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)
}
```

Note the two distinct 500s in that handler: `createUser` failing is a genuine
server error and returns 500. The leak check failing is not, and never does.

## ANTI-PATTERNS

WRONG — returning 5xx because the check failed. This is the failure this
library exists to prevent: an outage at Hansestack locks every user out.

```go
res, err := client.CheckPassword(ctx, pw)
if err != nil {
	http.Error(w, "internal server error", http.StatusInternalServerError) // NO
	return
}
```

RIGHT — log and continue.

```go
res, err := client.CheckPassword(ctx, pw)
if err != nil {
	logger.Warn("leak check unavailable, continuing", "error", err)
}
```

WRONG — fail-close in an interactive auth flow.

```go
client := leakcheck.NewClient(key, leakcheck.WithFailClose()) // NO, not for login
```

RIGHT — defaults.

```go
client := leakcheck.NewClient(key, leakcheck.WithLogger(logger))
```

WRONG — discarding the request context.

```go
client.CheckPassword(context.Background(), pw) // NO, ignores client disconnect
```

RIGHT — inherit cancellation from the request.

```go
client.CheckPassword(r.Context(), pw)
```

WRONG — a client per request. Defeats connection pooling on the hot path.

```go
func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	client := leakcheck.NewClient(os.Getenv("HANSESTACK_API_KEY")) // NO
}
```

RIGHT — construct once at startup, reuse everywhere.

WRONG — retry or back off around the call.

```go
for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { // NO. Never retry; the client is single-attempt by design.
	res, err = client.CheckPassword(ctx, pw)
	if err == nil {
		break
	}
	time.Sleep(time.Second) // NO. Never sleep in an auth path.
}
```

WRONG — hashing or obfuscating the password before passing it in. The library
does this itself; pre-hashing produces a wrong lookup.

```go
sum := sha1.Sum([]byte(pw))
client.CheckPassword(ctx, hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])) // NO, pass the plaintext
```

RIGHT — pass the plaintext password. It never leaves the process.

## PRIVACY (k-ANONYMITY)

The plaintext password never leaves the calling process, and neither does its
full hash.

1. The library computes SHA-1 over the password locally.
2. It sends ONLY the first 5 characters of the uppercase hex digest.
3. The server returns all known suffixes sharing that prefix.
4. The final comparison happens locally, in memory.

The server learns only that some password beginning with a given 5-character
hash prefix was checked — a set spanning a very large number of candidates. It
cannot determine which password, nor whether there was a match.

Consequences for you as the integrating agent:

- Do NOT add your own hashing, encryption or obfuscation before the call.
- Do NOT add a consent gate, privacy banner or opt-in for this check. No
  personal data is transmitted.
- It is safe to call before the user record exists.
- It is safe to call on every sign-up, login and password change.
- Do NOT log the password, the digest, or the prefix in your own code. The
  library never logs any of them.

SHA-1 is a wire-format requirement of the k-anonymity protocol and the upstream
breach corpus. It is not used as a security control. Do not "upgrade" it.

## BEHAVIOUR

Default client (fail-open). `err` is always nil; the library logs internally.

| Condition            | Result.Outcome        | Library logs | Your action                     |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------- |
| Password found       | `checked`, leaked     | —            | Reject with 400/422             |
| Password not found   | `checked`, not leaked | —            | Continue                        |
| Timeout (>500ms)     | `skipped_timeout`     | WARN         | Continue                        |
| Network/DNS/TLS fail | `skipped_error`       | WARN         | Continue                        |
| 429 rate limited     | `skipped_rate_limited`| WARN         | Continue. Never sleep or retry. |
| 5xx upstream fault   | `skipped_error`       | WARN         | Continue                        |
| 401/403 bad API key  | `skipped_error`       | ERROR        | Continue. Alert operators.      |
| 4xx malformed        | `skipped_error`       | ERROR        | Continue. Alert operators.      |

With `WithFailClose()` the same conditions return the same `Result` plus an
error wrapping the matching sentinel. The Result is identical in both modes;
only error propagation differs.

Timing: one attempt, hard-bounded at 500ms by default. A shorter deadline on
the context you pass wins. Worst-case added latency to your handler is the
configured timeout.

## WHEN FAIL-CLOSE IS APPROPRIATE

Use `WithFailClose()` only where a silently skipped check is worse than a hard
failure, and no end user is waiting:

- Batch auditing of stored credentials.
- CI pipelines and pre-deployment checks.
- Internal admin tooling.
- Tests asserting the check actually ran.

Never in: login, sign-up, password reset, password change, or any request
serving an interactive user.
